name: Pedro Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the office at a freight forwarding company, which means we arrange shipping for other firms' goods. We're about fifty people in a low building by the port, and I handle the managers' schedules, the customs paperwork filing, the booking of drivers' hotel rooms and all the supplier contracts. I sit by the window and watch the container cranes when the phones are quiet. It's not glamorous, but I like being the person who knows where everything is.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: When a ship's delayed and twenty bookings need moving at once. Last month a storm held up a vessel for four days, and I rebooked eleven hotel rooms and three trucks by lunchtime. I went home and slept for ten hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, useful in places but not the big deal people made it. At work I'd say the meeting-notes tool is handy and leave it there. With my mates at five-a-side I probably wouldn't bring it up at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine. Shipping goes up and down, but our firm's been around forty years and the owners are careful. My rent's fair, I've got about three months saved, and there are a couple of other forwarders nearby if this place ever went wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep using the AI for meeting notes and the odd email. I'd keep saving around two hundred a month. I'd also ask about the logistics certificate the company sponsors, because a step up into operations would mean more pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It'd be a normal sort of future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Trade slumps, mostly. In a bad year the firm freezes pay, and that happened when I'd just started. But they didn't cut admin, because the paperwork doesn't stop when trade slows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the logistics certificate get you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shot at an operations coordinator job, which pays about fifteen per cent more. It's two evenings a week for a year. I'd do it because it's sensible, not because I'm desperate.

At work I'd praise the **meeting-notes tool** and leave it there.
think: The firm is **careful** and forty years old, so I feel fine.
I have three months saved and **other forwarders** nearby if needed.
do: Keep using AI for **meeting notes** and the odd email.
Keep saving about **two hundred** a month.
Ask about the firm's sponsored **logistics certificate**.
S0.quote: The paperwork doesn't stop when trade slows.
fieldNote: He sees **trade slumps**, not AI, as the real risk in this world.
His **calm** rests on a careful employer and nearby options.
The certificate is a **sensible step**, not a fearful one.

steps.text: Keep using the AI meeting-notes tool at work
Save about two hundred a month
Apply for the firm's sponsored logistics certificate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have to adapt, and the smart ones will retrain people rather than just cut. I'd say the government should help with the cost of that, but not take over. At work I'd ask the managers straight out what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a lot of my job is on that list. Booking hotels, filing customs forms, checking contracts, answering supplier emails. I think the firm would keep me for a while because I know the place, but they wouldn't replace the two junior admins when they leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new booking and customs software properly in the first few months, because I'd rather be the one who runs it. I'd start the logistics certificate this year instead of next. I'd also put my savings up to three hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd stop feeling like the future was settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away. I'd look at the other forwarders' job adverts to see if they're asking for the same skills. If they're all cutting admin too, moving wouldn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents I'm fine and I'm learning the new systems, which would be true. My dad worked in the same warehouse for thirty years, so he'd ask why I don't just stay put. I'd have to explain that staying put might not be an option.

say: I'd say smart businesses **retrain people** rather than just cut.
I'd want government to **help with costs** but not take over.
think: Booking, filing customs forms and checking contracts are **on that list**.
They'd keep me but not replace the **two junior admins**.
do: Learn the new **booking and customs** software in the first months.
Start the **logistics certificate** this year instead of next.
Raise savings to **three hundred** a month.
feel: **Anxious**, no longer feeling the future is **settled**.
S1.quote: My dad worked in the same warehouse for thirty years, so he'd ask why I don't just stay put.

steps.text: Learn the firm's new booking and customs software first

Raise savings to three hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs a proper plan, fast, maybe some kind of wage support while people retrain. I'm not one for slogans, but this would be too big for firms to handle alone. At work I'd say we should be honest with each other about what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm out by 2028. Customs paperwork, booking and contracts are exactly the thinking work AGI does. The port's hands-on jobs, the crane drivers and warehouse staff, get three more years, but I'm not one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the warehouse manager about moving onto the floor, forklift licence and all, because that buys me until robots come around 2031. I'd cut my spending hard, no holiday, no new phone. And I'd look at moving back in with my parents to save rent if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Properly scared, which isn't like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving onto the warehouse floor. How would that feel after running the office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a step down, honestly. But I'd be earning, and I'd learn the physical side of the business. If I end up in operations later, having driven a forklift wouldn't hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said moving back in with your parents. How would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would be delighted and my dad would ask questions. I'd hate giving up my own place at twenty-eight. But saving nine hundred a month in rent would stretch everything.

say: I'd call for a proper **government plan**, like wage support during retraining.
At work I'd ask everyone to be **honest** about what's coming.
think: I'm **out by 2028**, because my work is exactly what AGI does.
The port's **hands-on jobs** get three more years, but I'm not one of them.
do: Ask to move onto the **warehouse floor** and get a forklift licence.
Cut spending hard: **no holiday**, no new phone.
Consider moving back with **his parents** to save rent.
S2.quote: Customs paperwork, booking and contracts are exactly the thinking work AGI does.
fieldNote: He uses the **robot delay** directly, by moving from desk to warehouse floor.
Taking a **step down** is a pragmatic choice he can accept.
His parents' house is the **backstop**, which he'd use reluctantly.

steps.text: Ask the warehouse manager for a floor job and forklift licence
Skip the holiday and the new phone this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but if firms and colleges work together it's doable. I'd say people shouldn't wait for the government. At work I'd suggest the firm trains office staff for operations now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my office job still goes, but five years means I could get into operations properly and maybe stay a bit longer. Operations is still partly thinking work though, so it's not safe either. I'd be juggling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the logistics certificate in year one and get the forklift licence too, so I've got both sides. I'd keep saving three hundred a month. I'd also stop thinking about buying a flat until I know where I'll be working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. Having two options calms me down a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why both the certificate and the forklift licence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't know which side lasts longer, the planning or the lifting. The licence is cheap, a week's course. It's an insurance policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend asking if they should take an admin job now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to take it but learn something with their hands on the side. Admin is a good way in, it's just not a good place to stay. That's what I'd do if I was twenty-two again.

I'd suggest the firm **trains office staff** for operations now.
think: I could move into **operations**, but that's partly thinking work too.
I'd be **juggling** two paths without knowing which lasts.

Put off **buying a flat** until his work is clearer.
feel: **Anxious** but busy, steadied by having **two options**.
S3.quote: Admin is a good way in, it's just not a good place to stay.
fieldNote: He hedges across **thinking and hands-on** work rather than betting on one.

steps.text: Finish the logistics certificate in the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to plan sensibly, and people shouldn't panic. At work I'd say we should use the time to train people properly. Online I'd say nothing, I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still expect my office job to go, but ten years is a long time to find a way through. I'd be thirty-seven. That's young enough to switch, old enough that I'd want to have done it by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the logistics certificate next year, and over a few years look at moving into port operations or maybe the harbour authority. I'd use the AI tools more as they come in, so I stay useful. I'd keep saving, and maybe buy a small flat in a few years if it looks stable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in the background. It's like knowing your lease ends but not exactly when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the harbour authority?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's public sector, so it's slower to cut, and there's a lot of safety and inspection work on the quays. Someone has to stand on the dock and sign things off. That might last longer than my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you feel calm in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knowing where I'll be working in 2036. If I got into the harbour authority by thirty, I'd feel much better. Until then it's on my mind.

At work I'd push to **train people** properly with the time.
think: My office job still **goes**, but ten years is long enough to find a way.
At **thirty-seven** I'd want to have switched already.

feel: **Anxious** in the background, like a lease ending at an **unknown date**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time to get off the desk. What would help is wage support while you retrain, and firms like mine offering floor or operations jobs to office people first. I'd take a step down if it meant a step forward later.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it would change the port itself. If trade gets cheaper and faster with AI, maybe there's more shipping, not less. I honestly don't know, and I don't think anyone does yet.

headlineQuote: I'd take a step down if it meant a step forward later.
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old** office administrator at a **freight forwarder** by the port.
He's **centre** and practical, wanting firms and **colleges** to share the work of retraining.
He's a **steady** adopter, using AI for meeting notes and learning new systems once they arrive.
He's **calm** in AI Plateau but **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, ready to move onto the warehouse floor.
He hedges between **operations** and hands-on work, with his parents' house as a **backstop**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have **no time** to get off the desk.
whatWouldHelp: **Wage support** while retraining, and firms offering office staff **floor jobs** first.
